newsitem.title: UK: Opportunities in Kenya seen despite IMF decision.
newsitem.headline: Opportunities in Kenya seen despite IMF decision.

text.p: International investors have been fleeing Kenya's financial markets but London-based analysts still see long-term investment opportunities.

While the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) decision last week to halt lending triggered a sharp drop in the country's currency and its stock markets, the prospect of elections possibly later this year should give a boost to investor confidence, they said.
The IMF suspended a $205 million three-year loan to Kenya, citing concerns over corruption and reform of the energy sector.

But analysts in London who follow Kenyan markets said securities such as Kenyan Treasury bills or the local stock market could again become lucrative, largely because of the significant economic progress the country has achieved in recent years.

"The IMF has just suspended the loan so the whole area looks like it is going down the Swanee, but of course it raises an interesting investment opportunity coming out the other side (of elections)," said a debt specialist at a U.S. investment bank in London.

Though Kenya is not expected to renegotiate a deal with the IMF immediately, some analysts believe the two sides would maintain a dialogue and that a lending programme would resume after the elections.

"Clearly the IMF letting the programme lapse is a dent to investor confidence. But I think there is a reasonable chance they will be able to renegotiate a program after the elections so that would be quite helpful to investor confidence," said Eric Lindenbaum, research analyst at Merrill Lynch & Co in London.
"Just as things turn bad quickly, I think things could look better quickly as well," Lindenbaum added.

The Merrill analyst said he believed "quiet contact" with the IMF was likely to continue because of the progress Kenya has made on the reform front over the years. "I don't think that is completely lost."
Analysts said dramatic improvement in Kenya's economic fundamentals should also help to stem some of the fallout from the IMF's decision to curtail lending.

"The whole Africa story is positive. Every Tom, Dick and Harry has gone and had a look at it and people who didn't even know how to locate places are going to have a look at it," added David McWilliams, analyst at BNP.
Of particular interest, analysts said, is Kenya's local Treasury bill market.
McWilliams said he sees good investment opportunties in the Treasury bill market given inflation is around six to 10 percent and economic growth expected to be five to 5-1/2 percent this year.
"The T-bills are interesting. They are about 15 percent, which is pretty good if you reckon the exchange rate will devalue by no more than a couple of percent," McWilliams said.
Prospects of a debt-for-equity swap -- where government debt would be converted into shares of state-controlled companies -- should also attract investor interest, analysts said.
There has been no official talk about such a plan but analysts see scope for a swap where buyers would receive a stream of income from the debt as well as an equity stake in Kenya's state-run assets.

"Most of the industry is in state hands so what they will say is if you buy Kenyan debt you can use that somewhere down the road to buy privatisations," said McWilliams, who believes the swap deal will occur by the end of the year.
"It sells the family's silver in return for its outstanding debt," he added.
